The authors made their code available, which allows reproducibility and exploration; this should be a requirement in the field but is not always complied with so we thank the authors for this. When applied to a limited set of TFs with ChIP-seq data in K562 cells, the authors predicted that TF pairs primarily bind to DNA with relaxed spacing between their TFBSs. Nevertheless, they were able to highlight already known as well as novel specific pairs of TF harboring constrained spacing. Next, the authors leveraged naturally occurring small insertions and deletions in the human population and mouse strains to confirm that altering spacing between TFBSs of TF pairs with relaxed spacing patterns has limited effect. This observation was further supported by synthetic spacing alterations induced by CRISPR-Cas9 experiments. The study is overall well designed and addresses an important challenge in our understanding of TF-DNA interactions and TF cooperation.

Nevertheless, we believe that there are some methodological limitations that favor the identification of relaxed spacing patterns, which should be better outlined in the manuscript to allow the reader to fully comprehend the results. From the title and first sections of the manuscript the readers are given the impression that relaxed and constrained spacing instances are about to be described and analysed with an equal importance. However, more focus is given to the relaxed spacing with both the mouse and CRISPR analyses exclusively dedicated to this with no clear explanation why. It would be useful to the readers to have this explicitly outlined by the authors. Finally, the terminology associated with TF-DNA interactions is very often incorrect, which confuses the readers and should be addressed. Please see below for our detailed comments.

1. The terminology associated with TF binding events is inappropriate. The authors use "ChIP-seq peaks", "TFBSs", and "motifs" almost interchangeably, which is not correct. The inconsistency in the terminology makes it difficult to fully comprehend what the authors meant/did.

An example is one of the first sentences in the Introduction: "TFs bind to short, degenerate sequences at promoters and enhancers, often referred to as TF binding motifs." The sequences bound by TFs in promoters and enhancers are TFBSs while TF binding motifs are computational representations of TFBS sets, which can be represented in many ways such as consensus motifs, PFMs, etc.

The next sentence claims that "TFs bind in an inter-dependent manner to closely spaced motifs." Motifs cannot be closely spaced but TFBSs are. Another example is the subsection "Motif identification" in the Methods section while the authors describe the prediction of TFBSs (using motifs).

2. More details should be provided to the Methods section. We acknowledge that the authors provide their code for inspection but outlining all methodological details in the manuscript would help in the clear understanding of the methods used. For instance:

a. The authors do not describe how they selected de novo motifs using HOMER (only best motif?, any p-value threshold?, any specific background used?)

b. For the TFBS predictions, the authors used a FPR threshold of 0.1%, but which was the specific tool that they used for that? FPR computation depends on background expectation, what was used (e.g. 25% A, C, G, or T or nucleotide composition of the genome)?

c. P. 23, lines 466-470. The authors described that they conducted a permutation test but then described that the null distribution was obtained using random spacing values between 0 and 100. If the null distribution is obtained by randomly selecting values between 0 and 100, it does not correspond to a permutation. A permutation test would imply permuting the observed spacing values.

d. P. 25, lines 513-516. It is not clear to us why the authors considered subsets of mutations when overlapping TFBSs predicted for the ChIP'ed TFs (only if 2-bit difference in motif score) but not for mutations overlapping TFBSs predicted by MAGGIE (all mutations). Why not consider all mutations in all cases?

3. The methodology used has several limitations that are not described by the authors. We encourage the authors to clearly outline them to the readers. Furthermore, we believe that these limitations favor the identification of relaxed spacing, which should be acknowledged, especially since the majority of the work focuses on alterations of spacing for TF pairs with relaxed spacing patterns.

a. It is well documented that TF binding preferences for TFs binding in close proximity (e.g. as dimers) can be altered. For instance, Jolma et al. (https://www.nature.com/articles/nature15518) used CAP-SELEX to reveal that "Most TF pair sites identified involved a large overlap between individual TF recognition motifs, and resulted in recognition of composite sites that were markedly different from the individual TF's motifs." As the authors relied on TF binding profiles (or motifs) corresponding to the binding preferences of TFs binding as monomers, it is possible that they will miss cooperative binding inducing a change in binding preferences. Furthermore, the authors did not consider overlapping motifs, which is again precluding the identification of constrained spacing.

b. The authors rely on ChIP-seq data to identify TF cooperation. While this is fine overall, this data does not allow the authors to know whether two identified TFs bind to their TFBSs on the same molecules. Indeed, ChIP-seq being a bulk experiment, it does not allow to discriminate between true co-occupancy on the same molecule or not. This should be discussed to put the work in a larger context to the readers. See https://www.cell.com/molecular-cell/pdf/S1097-2765(20)30793-0.pdf for a reference.

c. The de novo motif enrichment does not ensure that the motif found is actually the one bound by the ChIP'ed TF. Indeed, the motifs found for ARID1B and ARID2 correspond to GATA motifs while ARID TFs bind to more general A+T rich motifs. It is unclear whether the signal observed for these TFs is due to their direct interaction with DNA.

4. It would have been nice to perform similar experiments as the mouse and CRISPR ones but considering TF pairs with fixed spacing of their TFBSs. If the authors decide not to, they should at least clearly state to the readers that they more specifically focused on relaxed spacing and why.

5. It would have been interesting to provide information about the prevalence of cobinding events in the different ChIP-seq datasets. For instance, what is the percentage of ChIP-seq peaks that contain a predicted TFBS for each TF? What is the percentage of such peaks that contain cobinding events? Is there a difference in numbers b/w constrained or relaxed spacing. Providing this information would help the readers to put these observations into a more general context of TF binding regions.

6. It would be nice to have similar plots as in Figure 3B for pairs of TFs with constrained spacing to show how it contrasts.

7. In all analyses, it seems that more deletions than insertions were observed (see Figure 2A for instance). It would be interesting to see if the results recapitulate when considering insertions and deletions independently.

8. It is unclear to us what is the analysis of MAGGIE-predicted TFBSs adding to the story. Moreover, the authors claim that MAGGIE identifies "functional" TFBSs but the authors do not provide any specific evidence of function (and which function?) in our opinion.

9. It seems that there is a periodic pattern in Figure 5E with log-odds ratio periodically equal to 0 (at least with indel sizes < -45). Could this correspond to the minor groove width periodicity of ~10bp (see for instance https://www.cell.com/cell/pdf/S0092-8674(18)31312-6.pdf for periodicity of mutations)? Could the authors comment on that?

10. In several figures, the authors should provide all points instead of summarizing with boxplots, which are frowned upon as they hide data distribution.

11. P. 9 line 178: the authors mentioned 50 millions SNPs but we do not find where this data is used as observing SNPs would not alter spacing.

12. P. 2 line 46: "implicating their effect…" we would rather write "suggesting their effect…".

13. The authors seem to have ignored homodimers. Maybe their methodology could be extended to consider spacing b/w TFBSs for the same TF.

14. TF naming is sometimes inconsistent in the text and figures. For example, SPI1 and PU.1 are both used in Figure 3. Similarly, we recommend revisiting the text for p65 and RELA, as well as C/EBPβ and CEBPB.

15. It is not clear where the authors retrieved HepG2 cell line data from (used in the Figure 1 —figure supplement 4). Was this data processed in the same way as K562 cell line data?

16. P. 8 line 152: we suggest replacing "we overlaid" with "we mapped".

17. P. 1 line 30: "ChIP-sequencing" should be replaced with "ChIP-seq" for consistency.

18. Figure 3D,F,H : instead of motif score this should be TFBS score.

results.result: Genome-wide analysis of 73 TFs in K562 cells revealed that relaxed spacing relationships are the dominant pattern, with 45 TFs exclusively exhibiting relaxed spacing, 25 TFs participating in both relaxed and constrained interactions depending on partners, and only 3 TFs showing exclusively constrained spacing. Among 29 TF pairs with constrained spacing, most bind within 15 bp of each other.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C6 and C56-C57 provide converging computational evidence from ChIP-seq analysis of 73 TFs. The classification methodology is clearly described (C1), quantitative results are provided (C2-C5), and the finding that relaxed spacing dominates is consistently supported across multiple claims with specific numbers and statistical validation.

results.result: The study confirmed known constrained TF pairs (GATA1-TAL1, NFATC3-FOSL1) and identified novel constrained spacing patterns including MEF2A-JUND, CEBPB-TEAD4, and EGR1-JUND.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C8 and C58-C59 provide both validation of prior findings through citation and presentation of novel discoveries. The computational framework successfully identified both known composite motif pairs and previously unreported constrained relationships, with supporting data shown in figures.

results.result: TFs with relaxed spacing show progressively declining co-binding frequency with distance, this pattern is consistent across motif orientations and cell types, and binding activity is independent of spacing distance. Most relaxed spacing relationships are maintained in both repetitive and nonrepetitive regions, though some constrained pairs show region-specific patterns.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C15 provide multiple lines of evidence characterizing relaxed spacing relationships. The observations are supported by computational analysis across different conditions (motif orientations, cell types, genomic regions) with consistent findings and appropriate statistical tests (KS test mentioned in C22).

results.result: Analysis of >60 million InDels from gnomAD reveals that InDels between TF binding sites with constrained spacing are enriched for singletons and depleted for high-frequency variants, suggesting these spacing alterations are as deleterious as motif mutations. In contrast, InDels between relaxed TF pairs show patterns similar to background regions, suggesting weaker functional effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C16-C21 present a coherent analysis of human population genetics data. The size distributions (C16-C17), enrichment patterns (C18-C19), and functional inferences (C20-C21) are logically connected and supported by large-scale data. The inference about deleteriousness is appropriately qualified and based on established principles cited from prior work (Lek et al., 2016).

results.result: Analysis of natural genetic variation across five mouse strains shows that PU.1 and C/EBPβ exhibit relaxed spacing relationships with binding activity independent of spacing. Spacing alterations have smaller effect sizes on TF binding than motif mutations, with effects independent of InDel size or direction. Similar patterns are observed for both TFs and across promoters and enhancers.
results.evaluation: Claims C22-C31 present comprehensive analysis of natural variation with multiple independent strain comparisons. The statistical framework (KS test, Cohen's d effect sizes, Spearman correlations) is appropriate. The consistent findings across four pairwise comparisons and both TFs strengthen the conclusions. The observation that spacing effects are independent of InDel size (C27) while motif effects correlate with PWM score changes (C28) provides strong evidence for spacing tolerance.

results.result: The spacing tolerance observed for PU.1-C/EBPβ extends to hierarchical TF interactions (PU.1-p65, c-Jun-p65) and to downstream functional readouts including nascent transcription (GRO-seq) and histone acetylation (H3K27ac), with spacing alterations consistently showing weaker effects than motif mutations.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C36 extend the findings to additional TF pairs and functional readouts. The consistency across different experimental measures (ChIP-seq, GRO-seq, H3K27ac) and TF pairs strengthens the generality of the spacing tolerance phenomenon. The correlation analyses (C35) appropriately distinguish spacing effects from binding affinity effects.

results.result: Analysis of human endothelial cell QTLs shows that ERG and p65 exhibit relaxed spacing, with InDels altering spacing significantly depleted in bQTLs (Fisher's exact p=1.3e-15) compared to motif mutations which are enriched. Spacing alterations have smaller effect sizes than motif mutations for both p65 binding and H3K27ac in IL-1β-treated cells, and are not significantly different from likely non-functional variants.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C45 provide human cell-based validation using QTL data from dozens of individuals. The statistical evidence for depletion of spacing-altering InDels in QTLs (C41) is strong. The hierarchical interaction pattern (C44) is consistent with prior knowledge (C37). The effect size comparisons (C43, C45) appropriately use statistical tests and are consistent with the mouse data.

results.result: CRISPR/Cas9 mutagenesis at six endogenous loci between PU.1 and C/EBPβ binding sites generated InDels ranging from >30 bp deletions to short insertions. Spacing alterations (not overlapping motifs) had significantly weaker effects on TF binding than motif-overlapping deletions. At test regions #6 and #1, spacing alterations from 5 bp insertion to 22-41 bp deletion showed minimal effects on C/EBPβ and PU.1 binding, while motif-overlapping deletions substantially reduced binding.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C55 provide direct experimental validation through CRISPR mutagenesis. The experimental design is sound, testing six independent loci with a range of InDel sizes exceeding natural variation (C47). The odds ratio analysis appropriately compares ChIP-seq to input DNA. The consistency between natural variation at test region #1 (C53) and synthetic InDels (C54) strengthens the conclusions. Statistical significance is reported (C48) and specific examples are provided (C49, C51).

results.result: The findings are consistent with prior locus-specific studies of constrained spacing (interferon-β enhanceosome, Ciona enhancers) and recent single-molecule profiling showing lack of association between TF co-occupancy and precise spacing/orientation.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C61 and C64 appropriately place the current findings in context of prior literature. The citations are relevant and the comparisons are logical. The consistency with both structural studies of constrained interactions and recent single-molecule studies of relaxed interactions supports the validity of the computational classification approach.

results.result: The study's spacing analysis methodology has limitations: it does not consider overlapping TF binding sites and therefore cannot discover constrained TFs recognizing overlapping motifs or distinguish spacing alteration effects from effects on overlapping composite motifs.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C63 explicitly acknowledge methodological limitations. This is an appropriate and honest assessment that helps interpret the scope of the findings, particularly in comparison to prior in vitro studies (Jolma et al., 2015) that identified >300 TF-TF interactions including overlapping sites.

results.result: The dominance of relaxed spacing relationships has implications for enhancer/promoter selection mechanisms, suggesting that most TF collaborative binding does not require specific protein-protein interactions, though the mechanistic basis remains poorly understood.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C67 present interpretive statements about mechanistic implications. While the inference that relaxed spacing doesn't require specific protein-protein interactions (C66) is logical, it remains speculative without direct protein interaction data. The acknowledgment that mechanisms are poorly understood (C67) is appropriate but highlights the uncertain nature of these mechanistic claims.

results.result: The studies demonstrate clear tolerance of spacing alterations for TFs with relaxed spacing through both natural variation and CRISPR experiments. However, outliers exist where InDels between binding sites associate with significant TF binding differences, though at similar rates to regions without such InDels. Notably, bringing PU.1-C/EBPβ sites closer through deletions did not improve binding despite higher density of sites at closer distances.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C72 provide a balanced summary acknowledging both the main findings and limitations. The observation about outliers (C69) is important for interpreting generality. The paradox noted in C71-C72 (closer spacing in natural distribution but no improvement with deletions) is an interesting observation that suggests the spacing distribution may reflect other factors beyond optimal binding.

results.result: The spacing tolerance could potentially associate with high TF binding site turnover observed in prior studies, though this requires further investigation. A limitation is that few short insertions were obtained, preventing conclusions about tolerance of increased spacing.
results.evaluation: Claim C73 is appropriately speculative with acknowledgment that further work is needed. Claim C74 identifies a genuine experimental limitation - the CRISPR approach generated mostly deletions with few insertions, creating an asymmetry in the data. This limits conclusions about whether spacing increases are as well-tolerated as decreases.

results.result: The studies provide a framework for interpreting naturally occurring non-coding InDels: the majority (<5 bp) between relaxed TF pairs are unlikely to alter function, and even much longer InDels are frequently tolerated. In contrast, InDels between constrained TF pairs have potential for biological consequences. Application to disease-associated variants requires knowledge of relevant cell types and TF interaction types.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C80 present appropriate conclusions and applications of the findings. The size threshold (C76-C77) is well-supported by data from multiple sources. The distinction between relaxed and constrained pairs (C77-C79) is consistently demonstrated. The caveats about application to disease (C80) are appropriate and acknowledge the complexity of translating these findings to specific contexts.
